tier_reason: First-party README table produced by the repo's benchmark.sh (one /usr/bin/time run per case) on an Apple M2 Max; rustc version is not stated and the baseline is a prebuilt macOS system binary of unknown build, so not A. The column labelled 'GNU sort' is the macOS system sort, which is not GNU coreutils, so the claim against GNU sort is overstated.

corrections.baseline: macOS system /usr/bin/sort (Apple's BSD-derived sort shipped with macOS 15.5), labelled 'GNU sort (system)' in the README; benchmark.sh defaults REFERENCE_SORT to the system 'sort' and its own usage text labels /usr/bin/sort as BSD and /usr/local/bin/gsort as GNU. uutils (rust_coreutils) sort is a second column. Current GNU coreutils sort was not measured.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README table (seconds, macOS system sort labelled 'GNU sort' vs rust-sort, one timed run each): 1M lines -n 1.00 vs 0.03 (33.3x); 1M text 0.57 vs 0.03 (19.0x); 1M -rn 0.95 vs 0.03 (31.7x); 10M -n 6.21 vs 0.45 (13.8x); 10M text 6.00 vs 0.43 (14.0x); 10M -f 8.09 vs 0.42 (19.3x); 10M -g 24.17 vs 2.24 (10.8x); 10M -u 2.50 vs 0.55 (4.5x); 10M -s 3.28 vs 0.55 (6.0x); 100K rows are '>10x' to '>60x' from a '<0.01s' floor. Against uutils sort the same table gives 0.6x to 3.0x (rust-sort slower on -u and -s). performance_comparison_table.md has slightly different figures (1M -n 1.00 vs 0.04, 25.0x; 10M -n 6.26 vs 0.50, 12.5x). Headline 'up to 33x' (also written as 32x and 34x).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rust-sort: Cargo.toml [profile.release] opt-level = 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1, panic = abort; rustc version not stated (rust-version 1.70). Baseline: Apple's prebuilt system sort, build flags unknown.
corrections.workload: benchmark.sh: 100K, 1M and 10M lines generated deterministically with seq/awk (not random): numbers (i*7919) mod 32749 (at most 32749 distinct small integers), strings 'str_'+((i*13) mod 9973)+'_text' (9973 distinct values), floats and i mod 100 duplicates; flags -n, text, -rn, -u, -nu, -f, -R, -s, -g, -nru; each command timed once with /usr/bin/time -l (10 ms resolution) in the user's default locale.
corrections.caveats: Baseline mislabelled: the 'GNU sort (system)' column is the macOS system sort, which is Apple's BSD-derived sort, not GNU coreutils (benchmark.sh defaults to the system 'sort' and its usage text itself names /usr/bin/sort BSD and gsort GNU); eBay tsv-utils TipsAndTricks reports current GNU sort is often more than twice as fast as the macOS sort, and uutils sort beats the same column by about 8x at 10M lines, so the speedup over current GNU sort is probably far smaller than 33x. rust-sort runs rayon parallel sorts (par_sort_unstable_by, parallel radix and hash sort) above 8192 lines on a 12-core M2 Max against a single-process system sort. Test data are low-cardinality arithmetic sequences (at most 32749 distinct small integers, 9973 distinct strings), which suit its radix and hash paths, although the README says 'randomly generated'. Each case is one /usr/bin/time run with 10 ms resolution, though performance_comparison_table.md claims 'average of multiple runs'; the two result tables disagree slightly and both are dated December 2024 while the repo's code is from 2025. macOS only; not validated against the GNU coreutils test suite. LICENSE file is MIT while Cargo metadata says MIT OR Apache-2.0. 1 star; marketing-style README.
corrections.why_faster: From the sources: rayon parallel sorting above 8192 lines (par_sort_unstable_by and par_sort_by in core_sort.rs), radix sort for numeric keys (radix_sort.rs), hash-based grouping for -R (hash_sort.rs) and memory-mapped input (memmap2), compared with a single-process system sort; the gain is algorithmic and from parallelism, not from Rust codegen.

notes: Numbers match the README, but the baseline is the macOS system sort (BSD-derived), not GNU coreutils sort, so the 'faster than GNU sort' claim is untested; record shortcomings: mislabelled baseline, multi-threaded vs single-threaded, low-cardinality deterministic data, single 10 ms-resolution run, conflicting tables. Tier stays C; consider D if the orchestrator treats an off-baseline system sort as no valid measurement against GNU sort.

tier_reason: First-party hyperfine numbers in the README 'Selected Highlights' table with CPU named (i7-8550U) but no benchmark scripts in the repo (only src/ and tests/), no GNU versions, no build flags or locale; C.

corrections.caveats: Only 'selected highlights' are shown and every listed row is a win: 4 of the 9 rows compare against GNU (sort -n Linux and FreeBSD, sed Linux, cat|grep|wc Linux), the rest against BusyBox or FreeBSD native tools. No benchmark scripts or input files are in the repository (top level holds src/, tests/ and docs only), GNU versions, locale and build flags are not given, and the provenance of the 'GNU' sort used in the FreeBSD VM rows (139.5 ms vs 48.4 ms on Linux) is not stated. Inputs are 100k lines (10 ms to 30 ms runs, where process start-up matters). The sort -n fast path (src/commands/sort.rs sort_numeric_fast) parses each whole trimmed line with Rust's f64 parser (a line with a non-numeric suffix becomes 0, unlike GNU's leading-number parse), sorts with an unstable sort and has no last-resort whole-line comparison, so it does less work than GNU sort -n and can order ties differently. errata.md lists known shell parsing gaps. 1 star, crates.io 60 downloads.
corrections.why_faster: From src/commands/sort.rs: for whole-line keys sort -n parses each line once to f64 and runs sort_unstable_by on (value, index) pairs, and plain sort uses byte-order sort_unstable on whole lines, skipping GNU sort's general key extraction, locale collation and last-resort comparison; the gain is from simpler semantics and algorithm choice, not Rust codegen. No reason is given for the sed and pipeline rows.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated; Cargo.toml has no [profile.release] override (cargo default release opt-level 3). GNU builds are distribution binaries of unstated version.

notes: README numbers match the record. Small first-party claims (1.3x to 1.9x over GNU on Linux) with no published harness; the sort -n win comes partly from doing less than GNU -n (whole-line f64 parse, no tie-break comparison).

tier_reason: First-party wiki table (KyTea 219.6 ms, Vaporetto 29.0 ms, charwise 25.3 ms) with CPU and compiler versions but no optimisation flags and no benchmark script in the repo (evaluate/ measures accuracy); the arXiv 2406.17185 preprint and the NLP2022 paper are first-party and were seen only in search snippets, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'Vaporetto is 8.7 times faster than KyTea.' Wiki Speed-Comparison (Vaporetto v0.4.0, mean of 100 runs, ms): KyTea 219.6 (std 2.9), Vaporetto 29.0 (0.6), Vaporetto charwise 25.3 (0.4), so 7.6x and 8.7x (derived from page data); MeCab IPAdic 102.9 and UniDic 255.1, Lindera 397.1, sudachi.rs 286.2 and rust-tinysegmenter 272.7 use other dictionaries or models. arXiv 2406.17185 abstract: 5.7 times faster than the current approach based on the same model without loss of accuracy; NLP2022 paper: 5.4x vs KyTea (both snippet only).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.60.0 and GCC 11.2.0 (wiki); optimisation flags not stated for either side. The workspace Cargo.toml has no profile override (cargo release default opt-level 3); how KyTea was configured is not stated.
corrections.workload: Tokenizing the Aozora Bunko text of 'I Am a Cat' (Soseki Natsume), elapsed time measured 100 times (mean and std reported), KyTea and Vaporetto both using the KyTea compact SVM model based on BCCWJ and UniDic; whether model loading is excluded is not stated. Measured on Vaporetto v0.4.0 (wiki last edited 2022-06-09), not the current 0.6.5.
corrections.caveats: First-party wiki table from 2022 (Vaporetto v0.4.0) with a single corpus; no benchmark script is published (evaluate/ is an accuracy tool), build flags for both sides and whether model loading is excluded are not stated; the KyTea comparison is the only like-for-like row (same model); the 8.7x headline is the charwise variant (7.6x for the default mode), and the authors' own papers report smaller gains (5.7x in arXiv 2406.17185, 5.4x in NLP2022, snippet only). The speedup comes from a restructured inference algorithm, not from Rust versus C++.
corrections.why_faster: Algorithmic: the README's model-manipulation section shows that each pattern carries a precomputed weight array that is added to the character boundaries where the pattern occurs, and the pattern matching runs on a double-array Aho-Corasick automaton (daachorse), instead of KyTea's per-boundary feature extraction and weight lookup; the arXiv abstract attributes the 5.7x to this improved pointwise linear classification with the same model.

notes: Numbers match the wiki and README; record is accurate. For wave 14 the win is algorithmic (same model, different inference method), not language-level; the authors' papers give 5.7x (arXiv) and 5.4x (NLP2022) rather than the 8.7x headline.
